title: Mae Jemison: The First Black Woman in Space
summary:
On September 12, 1992, NASA astronaut Mae Jemison made history as the first African American woman to travel to space. She spent eight days in orbit aboard the space shuttle Endeavour, conducting 44 scientific experiments. But her journey to space was anything but ordinary.

Jemison was a medical doctor and engineer before joining NASA. She served in the Peace Corps as a medical officer in Sierra Leone and Liberia from 1983 to 1985. She earned a degree in chemical engineering from Stanford University and a doctorate in medicine from Cornell University. In 1987, NASA selected her as an astronaut candidate.

Her mission, STS-47, was the 50th space shuttle flight. As a mission specialist, Jemison oversaw experiments for Japan and the United States inside the Spacelab module. She also co-investigated a bone cell study. She logged over 190 hours in space before returning to Earth on September 20, 1992.

Jemison's inspiration came from an unlikely source: the TV show Star Trek. She was fascinated by Lt. Uhura, a Black woman in space. That character showed her that space was not off-limits. In 1993, Jemison's dream came full circle when she appeared as a lieutenant on Star Trek: The Next Generation.

Her historic flight was a milestone for NASA. In the agency's early days, women and people of color were never selected. NASA didn't send a woman to space until 1983, and the first Black man flew that same year. But it took another nine years for a Black woman to fly. Jemison retired from NASA in 1993 and founded the Jemison Group, a technology consulting firm. She continues to inspire future generations.
why_it_matters: Jemison's story shows that the people allowed to do science at the highest level have not always looked like everyone else — and that changing who gets a seat changes what the rest of us believe is possible.

background_read: NASA (the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, the U.S. government agency that runs the country's space program) was created in 1958, at the start of the Space Age.
For decades its astronaut corps was made up almost completely of white men, many of them military test pilots.
That began to change in the 1980s, when Sally Ride became the first American woman in space and Guion Bluford became the first African American man in space, both flying during the same year.

Jemison's inspiration came from Star Trek (a science-fiction TV series that first aired in the 1960s and imagined a future where humans of all backgrounds worked together in space), especially the character Lt. Uhura, played by Nichelle Nichols.
The Peace Corps (a U.S. volunteer service started in the early 1960s under President John F. Kennedy) sends Americans abroad to work on health, education, and development projects.

perspectives.description: Jemison proved that a Black woman could be an astronaut, opening the door for others and showing that talent can come from any background. Her unusual mix of medicine, engineering, and volunteer service showed that there is more than one route into space.

perspectives.perspective: Critical of how slow the change was
perspectives.description: Supporters of diversity point out that a 'first' is also a sign of how long exclusion lasted: for decades NASA selected only white men, and the milestone came only after years of pressure. Counting firsts shows how far institutions still have to go.

Jemison's career reflects a broader shift in NASA's astronaut corps from mostly test pilots to scientists and doctors with research specialties. Her work as a mission specialist on experiments, rather than as a pilot, shows how the job itself was changing.

After NASA, Jemison founded a technology company and kept working on science education and outreach. The next question is whether the children who see her story will actually get the training and opportunities to follow her path.
